claim: Fanconi anemia (FA) is a childhood syndrome that results in bone marrow failure, leukemia and head and neck cancers.
source: Fanconi anemia (FA) is a devastating childhood syndrome that results in bone marrow failure, leukemia and head and neck cancers (Gillio et al., 1997; Butturini et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gillio et al., 1997 and Butturini et al., 1994

claim: FA is caused by inheritance of one of 22 dysfunctional FA genes (FANCA-FANCW).
source: FA is caused by inheritance of one of 22 dysfunctional FA genes (FANCA-FANCW) (Tan and Deans, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tan and Deans, 2017

claim: Absence of any one member of the FA pathway causes genome instability during DNA replication.
source: Absence of any one member of the pathway causes genome instability during DNA replication, which results in mutagenic (cancer-causing) DNA damage and hypersensitivity to chemotherapeutic (normal and cancer-killing) DNA damage (Deans and West, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deans and West, 2011

claim: The conjugation of ubiquitin to FANCI:FANCD2 (ID2) complexes is central to the FA pathway.
source: Central to the FA pathway is the conjugation of ubiquitin to FANCI:FANCD2 (ID2) complexes (Walden and Deans, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Walden and Deans, 2014

claim: ID2 monoubiquitination is critical to prevention of bone marrow failure in FA.
source: ID2 monoubiquitination is critical to prevention of bone marrow failure in FA, but it is currently unknown how ID2-ub differs in its function to ID2.
evidence: Statement of established importance of ID2 monoubiquitination in FA pathology

claim: FAN1 nuclease was proposed to interact with FANCD2Ub via its ubiquitin-binding domain (UBZ).
source: For example, FAN1 nuclease was proposed to interact with FANCD2Ub via its ubiquitin-binding domain (UBZ) (Smogorzewska et al., 2010), whereas recruitment of SLX4 endonuclease to the interstrand crosslink site was shown to be dependent on FANCD2 ubiquitination (Klein Douwel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smogorzewska et al., 2010

claim: Recruitment of SLX4 endonuclease to the interstrand crosslink site was shown to be dependent on FANCD2 ubiquitination.
source: For example, FAN1 nuclease was proposed to interact with FANCD2Ub via its ubiquitin-binding domain (UBZ) (Smogorzewska et al., 2010), whereas recruitment of SLX4 endonuclease to the interstrand crosslink site was shown to be dependent on FANCD2 ubiquitination (Klein Douwel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Klein Douwel et al., 2014

claim: The retention of FANCD2 in chromatin foci is dependent on its monoubiquitination by a 'core complex' of Fanconi anemia proteins.
source: The retention of FANCD2 in chromatin foci is dependent on its monoubiquitination by a 'core complex' of Fanconi anemia proteins (Walden and Deans, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Walden and Deans, 2014

claim: FANCI and the FA core complex are required to generate FANCD2-foci that mark the location of double strand breaks, stalled replication forks and R-loops in the nucleus.
source: FANCI and the FA core complex are required to generate FANCD2-foci that mark the location of double strand breaks, stalled replication forks and R-loops (Taniguchi et al., 2002; Schwab et al., 2015; Wienert et al., 2019) in the nucleus, and protect nascent DNA at these sites from degradation by cellular nucleases (Schlacher et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Taniguchi et al., 2002; Schwab et al., 2015; Wienert et al., 2019

claim: FANCD2-foci protect nascent DNA at double strand breaks, stalled replication forks and R-loops from degradation by cellular nucleases.
source: FANCI and the FA core complex are required to generate FANCD2-foci that mark the location of double strand breaks, stalled replication forks and R-loops (Taniguchi et al., 2002; Schwab et al., 2015; Wienert et al., 2019) in the nucleus, and protect nascent DNA at these sites from degradation by cellular nucleases (Schlacher et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schlacher et al., 2012

claim: The ubiquitinated forms of FANCD2 and FANCI become resistant to detergent and high-salt extraction from chromatin foci.
source: The ubiquitinated form of FANCD2, and also its ubiquitinated partner protein FANCI, become resistant to detergent and high-salt extraction from these foci (Smogorzewska et al., 2007; Montes de Oca et al., 2005), leading to speculation about the existence of a chromatin anchor or altered DNA binding specificity post-monoubiquitination (Longerich et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smogorzewska et al., 2007; Montes de Oca et al., 2005

claim: A DNA interacting domain is required for FANCI:FANCD2 binding to DNA.
source: A recent electron microscopy study revealed a DNA interacting domain that is required for FANCI:FANCD2 binding to DNA (Liang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liang et al., 2016

claim: The monoubiquitination sites of FANCI:FANCD2 are buried and inaccessible in the dimer interface of the complex.
source: The crystal structure of the non-ubiquitinated FANCI:FANCD2 shows that the monoubiquitination sites of FANCI:FANCD2 are buried and therefore inaccessible in the dimer interface of the complex (Joo et al., 2011), suggesting that DNA binding might be required to expose the ubiquitin binding sites.
evidence: Supported by citation to Joo et al., 2011

claim: Non-ubiquitinated FANCI and FANCD2 preferentially bind to branched DNA molecules which mimic DNA replication and repair intermediates.
source: Based on biochemical analyses, non-ubiquitinated FANCI and FANCD2 preferentially bind to branched DNA molecules which mimic DNA replication and repair intermediates (Longerich et al., 2014; Longerich et al., 2009; Niraj et al., 2017); however, how that activates monoubiquitination of FANCI:FANCD2 remains poorly understood.
evidence: Supported by citations to Longerich et al., 2014; Longerich et al., 2009; Niraj et al., 2017

claim: DNA is a cofactor for maximal ubiquitination of FANCI:FANCD2.
source: DNA is a cofactor for maximal ubiquitination (Longerich et al., 2014; van Twest et al., 2017), as is phosphorylation by the ATR kinase (Tan et al., 2020b; Ishiai et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Longerich et al., 2014; van Twest et al., 2017

claim: Phosphorylation by the ATR kinase is a cofactor for maximal ubiquitination of FANCI:FANCD2.
source: DNA is a cofactor for maximal ubiquitination (Longerich et al., 2014; van Twest et al., 2017), as is phosphorylation by the ATR kinase (Tan et al., 2020b; Ishiai et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tan et al., 2020b; Ishiai et al., 2008

claim: None of the tested proteins containing ubiquitin binding domains showed increased affinity for monoubiquitinated FANCI:FANCD2 over non-ubiquitinated FANCI:FANCD2.
source: Surprisingly, our main observation was that none of the proteins showed any increased affinity for IUbD2Ub over ID2 (Figure 1d).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1d comparing binding of proteins to ubiquitinated vs non-ubiquitinated ID2

claim: Monoubiquitination of FANCI:FANCD2 leads to DNA mobility shifts in EMSA even at low concentrations.
source: ID2 monoubiquitination readily lead to DNA mobility shifts using EMSA (electromobility shift assay) even at low concentrations, but this was not observed for the unmodified (apo)-ID2 complex in the absence of the enzymatically active FA core complex, or when monoubiquitination-defective K-to-R mutants of ID2 were used in the reaction (Figure 2c, lanes 2–4).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2c demonstrating DNA mobility shifts with monoubiquitinated ID2

claim: Unmodified FANCI:FANCD2 complex does not cause DNA mobility shifts in EMSA in the absence of enzymatically active FA core complex.
source: ID2 monoubiquitination readily lead to DNA mobility shifts using EMSA (electromobility shift assay) even at low concentrations, but this was not observed for the unmodified (apo)-ID2 complex in the absence of the enzymatically active FA core complex, or when monoubiquitination-defective K-to-R mutants of ID2 were used in the reaction (Figure 2c, lanes 2–4).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2c showing no DNA mobility shifts with unmodified ID2

claim: Monoubiquitination-defective K-to-R mutants of FANCI:FANCD2 do not cause DNA mobility shifts in EMSA.
source: ID2 monoubiquitination readily lead to DNA mobility shifts using EMSA (electromobility shift assay) even at low concentrations, but this was not observed for the unmodified (apo)-ID2 complex in the absence of the enzymatically active FA core complex, or when monoubiquitination-defective K-to-R mutants of ID2 were used in the reaction (Figure 2c, lanes 2–4).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2c showing no DNA mobility shifts with K-to-R mutants

claim: Various different dsDNA-containing structures can robustly stimulate ID2 monoubiquitination.
source: Previously, we and others showed that various different dsDNA-containing structures could robustly stimulate ID2 monoubiquitination (Longerich et al., 2014; van Twest et al., 2017; Sareen et al., 2012), but that single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) does not.
evidence: Supported by citations to Longerich et al., 2014; van Twest et al., 2017; Sareen et al., 2012

claim: Single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) does not robustly stimulate ID2 monoubiquitination.
source: Previously, we and others showed that various different dsDNA-containing structures could robustly stimulate ID2 monoubiquitination (Longerich et al., 2014; van Twest et al., 2017; Sareen et al., 2012), but that single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) does not.
evidence: Supported by citations to Longerich et al., 2014; van Twest et al., 2017; Sareen et al., 2012

claim: Non-ubiquitinated ID2 exhibits high affinity toward 3' flap DNA structure.
source: Interestingly, non-ubiquitinated ID2 also exhibited high affinity toward 3' flap DNA structure (similar to a replication fork stalled on the lagging strand), which has been previously observed (Liang et al., 2016).
evidence: Experimental observation in this study, with citation to Liang et al., 2016 for previous observation

claim: The 3'-Flap structure and other dsDNA containing structures lead to increased ID2 monoubiquitination and increased retention of an EMSA shifted band.
source: The 3'-Flap structure, and each of the other dsDNA containing structures, led to increased ID2 monoubiquitination and increased retention of an EMSA shifted band (Figure 3).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: Single-stranded DNA does not cause an EMSA shift despite stimulating monoubiquitination to similar levels at long time points.
source: Conversely, ssDNA, which stimulates monoubiquitination more slowly (van Twest et al., 2017) but to similar levels at the long time point of this assay, did not cause an EMSA shift.
evidence: Experimental observation with citation to van Twest et al., 2017

claim: The gel shifted DNA band contains both FANCI and FANCD2 proteins.
source: First, western blotting of the EMSA gels confirmed that the gel shifted DNA band contains both FANCI and FANCD2 proteins (Figure 4a).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4a using western blotting

claim: FANCIUb still co-immunoprecipitates with FANCD2Ub at the plateau of the in vitro ubiquitination reaction.
source: Second, FANCIUb still co-immunoprecipitated with FANCD2Ub at the plateau of the in vitro ubiquitination reaction (Figure 4b).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4b using co-immunoprecipitation

claim: Monoubiquitination of FANCI:FANCD2 does not lead to dissociation of the heterodimer in vitro.
source: In contrast, we did not observe any Ub-mediated dissociation of ID2 in vitro.
evidence: Experimental observation from this study

claim: FANCIKR:FANCD2WT or FANCIWT:FANCD2KR mutants result in decreased EMSA shift.
source: FANCIKR:FANCD2WT or FANCIWT:FANCD2KR mutant results in decrease in EMSA shift, and FANCIKR:FANCD2KR did not bind to DNA (Figure 4c).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4c

claim: FANCIKR:FANCD2KR did not bind to DNA.
source: FANCIKR:FANCD2WT or FANCIWT:FANCD2KR mutant results in decrease in EMSA shift, and FANCIKR:FANCD2KR did not bind to DNA (Figure 4c).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4c

claim: Retention of FANCI:FANCD2 on DNA correlates with the extent of FANCD2 monoubiquitination.
source: However, this retention on DNA correlated with the extent of FANCD2 monoubiquitination retained by these mutant complexes.
evidence: Experimental observation from mutant analysis

claim: Both FANCD2 and FANCI are found in the EMSA shifted product, in higher amounts when both proteins are capable of being monoubiquitinated.
source: Western blotting the EMSA gels confirmed that both FANCD2 and FANCI are found in the EMSA shifted product, although in higher amounts when both proteins are capable of being monoubiquitinated (Figure 4d).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4d using western blotting

claim: Ubiquitin mutants F4A, D58A, I44A, V70A, K11R, and L73P were conjugated to ID2 by the FA core complex with similar efficiency.
source: Each of these Ub mutants were conjugated to ID2 by the FA core complex with similar efficiency (Figure 5b) and their clamping onto DNA was then measured.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5b

claim: Mutations in ubiquitin surface patch 1 (F4A, D58A), surface patch 2 (I44A, V70A), a DNA binding residue (K11R) or a tail mutant (L73P) had no apparent effect on DNA clamping.
source: Mutations in surface patch 1 (F4A, D58A), surface patch 2 (I44A, V70A), a DNA binding residue (K11R) or a tail mutant (L73P) had no apparent effect on DNA clamping (Figure 5c).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5c

claim: No canonical surface or region of ubiquitin is critical for DNA clamping of ID2.
source: This result suggests that no canonical surface or region of ubiquitin is critical for DNA clamping of ID2, and instead ubiquitin conjugation to ID2 probably induces a conformational rearrangement of the heterodimer.
evidence: Inference from experimental results with ubiquitin mutants

claim: Ubiquitin conjugation to ID2 probably induces a conformational rearrangement of the heterodimer.
source: This result suggests that no canonical surface or region of ubiquitin is critical for DNA clamping of ID2, and instead ubiquitin conjugation to ID2 probably induces a conformational rearrangement of the heterodimer.
evidence: Inference from experimental results with ubiquitin mutants

claim: Monoubiquitinated FANCI:FANCD2 complex is recovered only when FANCI is monoubiquitinated using Avi-tag ubiquitin purification.
source: We recovered monoubiquitinated FANCI:FANCD2 complex only when FANCI is monoubiquitinated, suggesting that the N-terminus of D2-attached ubiquitin may be buried within the di-ubiquitinated complex, but the N-terminus of ubiquitin attached to FANCI is accessible for avidin binding (Figure 6b).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6b

claim: The N-terminus of FANCD2-attached ubiquitin may be buried within the di-ubiquitinated complex.
source: We recovered monoubiquitinated FANCI:FANCD2 complex only when FANCI is monoubiquitinated, suggesting that the N-terminus of D2-attached ubiquitin may be buried within the di-ubiquitinated complex, but the N-terminus of ubiquitin attached to FANCI is accessible for avidin binding (Figure 6b).
evidence: Inference from purification results shown in Figure 6b

claim: The N-terminus of ubiquitin attached to FANCI is accessible for avidin binding.
source: We recovered monoubiquitinated FANCI:FANCD2 complex only when FANCI is monoubiquitinated, suggesting that the N-terminus of D2-attached ubiquitin may be buried within the di-ubiquitinated complex, but the N-terminus of ubiquitin attached to FANCI is accessible for avidin binding (Figure 6b).
evidence: Inference from purification results shown in Figure 6b

claim: FANCIub:FANCD2ub forms filament-like arrays when bound to dsDNA plasmid.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that FANCIub:FANCD2ub forms filament-like arrays when bound to dsDNA plasmid (Figure 6c).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6c using electron microscopy

claim: Filament-like arrays were not observed in unmodified FANCI:FANCD2 protein preparation in the absence or presence of plasmid DNA.
source: Such arrays were not observed in the unmodified FANCI:FANCD2 protein preparation in the absence of presence of plasmid DNA, nor in previous investigations of human or Xenopus FANCI:FANCD2 complexes studied by EM (Figure 6d–e and Swuec et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2016; Lopez-Martinez et al., 2019).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6d-e and citations to previous studies

claim: No filament-like structures were observed when monoubiquitinated FANCI:FANCD2 was bound to 60 bp DNA.
source: When smaller DNA molecules were used as the substrate for ID2 binding, we either observed no filament-like structures (60 bp, Figure 7a) or shorter filament-like structures (150 bp, Figure 7b) compared to structures that were on average 7-8x longer than the characteristic double saxophone structure of ID2 heterodimer in the non-ubiquitinated state (Figure 7c).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7a

claim: Shorter filament-like structures were observed when monoubiquitinated FANCI:FANCD2 was bound to 150 bp DNA.
source: When smaller DNA molecules were used as the substrate for ID2 binding, we either observed no filament-like structures (60 bp, Figure 7a) or shorter filament-like structures (150 bp, Figure 7b) compared to structures that were on average 7-8x longer than the characteristic double saxophone structure of ID2 heterodimer in the non-ubiquitinated state (Figure 7c).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7b

claim: Filament-like structures on plasmid DNA were on average 7-8x longer than the characteristic double saxophone structure of ID2 heterodimer in the non-ubiquitinated state.
source: When smaller DNA molecules were used as the substrate for ID2 binding, we either observed no filament-like structures (60 bp, Figure 7a) or shorter filament-like structures (150 bp, Figure 7b) compared to structures that were on average 7-8x longer than the characteristic double saxophone structure of ID2 heterodimer in the non-ubiquitinated state (Figure 7c).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7c

claim: Array length correlates with the size of DNA available for ID2 binding.
source: The observation that array length correlated with the size of DNA available for ID2 binding strongly suggested that the association between heterodimer subunits in the array was DNA-mediated.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations with different DNA lengths

claim: The association between heterodimer subunits in the array is DNA-mediated.
source: The observation that array length correlated with the size of DNA available for ID2 binding strongly suggested that the association between heterodimer subunits in the array was DNA-mediated.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations with different DNA lengths

claim: Addition of Benzonase breaks the long arrays formed by IubD2ub complex into very short or heterodimer-sized units.
source: It is apparent from EM images that addition of Benzonase breaks the long arrays formed by IubD2ub complex into very short or heterodimer-sized units (Figure 7d).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7d

claim: Benzonase cleaves exposed DNA between IubD2ub units, leading to destabilization of the filamentous arrays.
source: This finding is consistent with Benzonase cleaving exposed DNA between IubD2ub units, leading to destabilization of the filamentous arrays.
evidence: Inference from Benzonase treatment results

claim: Ubiquitination of ID2 leads to a ubiquitin- and DNA-stabilized filament-like structure in vitro.
source: Together our results show that, in vitro, ubiquitination of ID2 leads to a ubiquitin- and DNA- stabilized filament-like structure.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from this study

claim: The IubD2ub complex forms a distinct architecture from that of ID2.
source: These particles were similar in size to non-ubiquitinated ID2, but it is clear from individual molecule and class average views that the IubD2ub complex forms a distinct architecture from that of ID2 (Figure 7e–f).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7e-f from EM analysis

claim: The overall shape of IubD2ub particles reveals a twisting that repositions the solenoid arms of one or both of the subunits bringing them into closer proximity.
source: In particular, the overall shape of individual particles and their class averages reveal a twisting that repositions the solenoid arms of one or both of the subunits bringing them into closer proximity.
evidence: Observation from EM class averages

claim: The conformational change induced by monoubiquitination appears to reduce the size of ID2 in one direction (x vs y) but not the other.
source: The conformational change induced appears to reduce the size of ID2 in one direction (x vs y) but not the other (Figure 7g–h), similar to that predicted in a previously proposed model that placed DNA in a channel between FANCI and FANCD2 post DNA binding (Longerich et al., 2014).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7g-h with citation to Longerich et al., 2014

claim: Monoubiquitination induces a conformational change in the ID2 complex that clamps it upon DNA.
source: These images support the view that monoubiquitination induces a conformational change in the ID2 complex that clamps it upon DNA.
evidence: Inference from EM structural analysis

claim: Monoubiquitination of FANCI:FANCD2 by the FA core complex is the central event in the FA-BRCA DNA repair pathway.
source: Monoubiquitination of FANCI:FANCD2 by the FA core complex is the central event in this pathway.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about the FA pathway

claim: Monoubiquitination directly clamps the ID2 complex onto double-stranded DNA.
source: Here, we showed that monoubiquitination directly clamps the ID2 complex onto double-stranded DNA, and promotes a filament-like coating of long DNA molecules.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from this study

claim: Monoubiquitination promotes a filament-like coating of long DNA molecules by ID2.
source: Here, we showed that monoubiquitination directly clamps the ID2 complex onto double-stranded DNA, and promotes a filament-like coating of long DNA molecules.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from this study

claim: Fork protection involves exclusion of cellular nucleases such as MRE11 and DNA2 from the stalled DNA replication fork.
source: 'Fork protection' involves (i) exclusion of cellular nucleases such as MRE11 and DNA2 from the stalled DNA replication fork, and (ii) specific recruitment of other factors that are able to restart DNA replication (Schlacher et al., 2012; Tian et al., 2017; Madireddy et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schlacher et al., 2012; Tian et al., 2017; Madireddy et al., 2016

claim: Fork protection involves specific recruitment of factors that are able to restart DNA replication.
source: 'Fork protection' involves (i) exclusion of cellular nucleases such as MRE11 and DNA2 from the stalled DNA replication fork, and (ii) specific recruitment of other factors that are able to restart DNA replication (Schlacher et al., 2012; Tian et al., 2017; Madireddy et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schlacher et al., 2012; Tian et al., 2017; Madireddy et al., 2016

claim: Inhibition of either MRE11 or DNA2 nucleases can significantly alleviate the sensitivity of FA-BRCA mutant cells to replication stalling agents.
source: The role of nuclease exclusion seems most important because inhibition of either of two nucleases, MRE11 or DNA2, can significantly alleviate the sensitivity of FA-BRCA mutant cells to replication stalling agents (Schlacher et al., 2012; Tian et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schlacher et al., 2012; Tian et al., 2017

claim: IUbD2Ub does not demonstrate restricted interaction with any specific protein partner.
source: We propose that IUbD2Ub does not demonstrate restricted interaction with any specific protein partner.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental findings in this study

claim: Retention of IUbD2Ub in chromatin after ubiquitination would bring the complex into proximity of DNA repair factors where it could influence their activity.
source: None-the-less, its retention in chromatin after ubiquitination would be much more likely to bring the complex into proximity of these other DNA repair factors, where it could still influence their activity.
evidence: Inference from experimental findings

claim: Clamping onto DNA occurs through a ubiquitin-mediated conformational change in the ID2 complex.
source: Clamping onto DNA occurs through a ubiquitin-mediated conformational change in the ID2 complex.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from this study

claim: A ubiquitin binding-domain (UBD) in FANCD2 has been shown necessary for the retention of the protein in the chromatin fraction and for strong binding to FANCI.
source: A ubiquitin binding-domain (UBD) in FANCD2 has previously been shown necessary for the retention of the protein in the chromatin faction, and for strong binding to FANCI (Rego et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rego et al., 2012

claim: The UBD domain in FANCD2 most likely mediates the clamping function and conformational rearrangement.
source: This UBD domain sits in the FANCD2 structure opposite to where ubiquitin is likely to reside after its conjugation on to FANCI by the FA core complex, and most likely mediates the clamping function and conformational rearrangement.
evidence: Inference from structural information and experimental findings

claim: A high-resolution cryo-EM structure of chicken ID2Ub uncovered a conformational rearrangement of ID2 that is stapled in place by ubiquitin:UBD association.
source: A high-resolution cryo-EM structure of chicken ID2Ub published by Alcón et al alongside our study (Alcón et al., 2020), also uncovered a conformational rearrangement of ID2 that is then stapled in place by ubiquitin:UBD association.
evidence: Supported by citation to Alcón et al., 2020

claim: Histone H2A shows an increased association with DNA after monoubiquitination.
source: Other DNA-binding proteins such as histone H2A show an increased association with DNA after monoubiquitination (Zhang, 2003) and monoubiquitination also increases the DNA occupancy of transcription factors such as FOXO4 and CIITA (Greer et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang, 2003

claim: Monoubiquitination increases the DNA occupancy of transcription factors such as FOXO4 and CIITA.
source: Other DNA-binding proteins such as histone H2A show an increased association with DNA after monoubiquitination (Zhang, 2003) and monoubiquitination also increases the DNA occupancy of transcription factors such as FOXO4 and CIITA (Greer et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Greer et al., 2003

claim: Ubiquitin to UBD mediated clamping may be a general mechanism of protein:DNA target stabilization.
source: It is possible that ubiquitin to UBD mediated clamping is a general mechanism of protein:DNA target stabilization.
evidence: Speculation based on findings in this study and other systems

claim: Fourier Transformation of the EM images did not reveal clear evidence for layer lines expected for fiber diffraction.
source: Fourier Transformation of the EM images did not reveal clear evidence for layer lines, that are expected for fiber diffraction, so we expect that the IUbD2Ub is not a true filament.
evidence: Analysis of EM data

claim: IUbD2Ub is not a true filament.
source: Fourier Transformation of the EM images did not reveal clear evidence for layer lines, that are expected for fiber diffraction, so we expect that the IUbD2Ub is not a true filament.
evidence: Inference from Fourier Transformation analysis

claim: The length of plasmid-associated IUbD2Ub structures is on average 7-8x (but up to 40x) that associated with 60 bp DNA.
source: On average, the length of plasmid-associated structures is 7-8x (but up to 40x) that of that associated with 60 bp DNA.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of EM data

claim: IUbD2Ub binding to DNA is flexible and can adopt multiple conformations, akin to RPA binding and protecting ssDNA.
source: The modular nature of IUbD2Ub arrays suggests that IUbD2Ub binding to DNA is flexible and can adopt multiple conformations, akin to RPA binding and protecting ssDNA (Yates et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference from EM observations with citation to Yates et al., 2018

claim: Antibodies against FANCD2 have been used as a marker of double strand breaks, stalled replication forks and R-loops because the protein forms large, intensely stained foci during S-phase that are increased after treatment with DNA damaging agents.
source: Antibodies against FANCD2 have long been used as a marker of double strand breaks, stalled replication forks and R-loops because the protein forms large, intensely stained foci during S-phase that are increased after treatment with DNA damaging agents (Taniguchi et al., 2002; Schwab et al., 2015; Deans and West, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Taniguchi et al., 2002; Schwab et al., 2015; Deans and West, 2009

claim: FANCD2 foci are due to coating of DNA around damaged forks, potentially in filamentous arrays.
source: We suspect that these intense foci are due to coating of DNA around damaged forks, potentially in filamentous arrays similar to those we observed by EM.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings

claim: FANCD2 and γH2AX showed no specific localization in a bulk population of cells, but strongly localized adjacent to a Cas9-induced site-specific DNA break.
source: FANCD2, and two other damage markers MRE11 and γH2AX, showed no specific localization in a bulk population of cells, but strongly localized adjacent to a Cas9-induced site-specific DNA break.
evidence: Description of ChIP-Seq results

claim: Both γH2AX and FANCD2 produced a broad peak centered at the target site kilobases (kb) to megabases (mb) in length in ChIP-Seq.
source: Both γH2AX and FANCD2 produced a broad peak centered at the target site kilobases (kb) to megabases (mb) in length.
evidence: Description of ChIP-Seq results

claim: MRE11 is located within a very tight peak within ~100 bp of the break in ChIP-Seq.
source: In contrast, MRE11 is located within a very tight peak within ~100 bp of the break.
evidence: Description of ChIP-Seq results

claim: Chromatin within 1–2 kb of the DSB showed reduced occupancy by γH2AX, consistent with dechromatinization around break sites.
source: Chromatin within 1–2 kb of the DSB showed reduced occupancy by γH2AX, consistent with dechromatinization around break sites (Iacovoni et al., 2010), but FANCD2 was present right up to the DSB.
evidence: Description of ChIP-Seq results with citation to Iacovoni et al., 2010

claim: FANCD2 was present right up to the DSB in ChIP-Seq.
source: Chromatin within 1–2 kb of the DSB showed reduced occupancy by γH2AX, consistent with dechromatinization around break sites (Iacovoni et al., 2010), but FANCD2 was present right up to the DSB.
evidence: Description of ChIP-Seq results

claim: Accumulation of FANCD2 increases at the DSB early after cleavage, and accumulates more distant from the DSB progressively with time post-cleavage.
source: Accumulation of FANCD2 increases at the DSB early after cleavage, and accumulates more distant from the DSB progressively with time post-cleavage.
evidence: Description of ChIP-Seq results

claim: The progressive accumulation of FANCD2 is suggestive of a polymerization of the FANCD2 signal away from the break site.
source: This is suggestive of a polymerization of the FANCD2 signal away from the break site, as we hypothesize would occur for a protein that forms a growing array of molecules at broken DNA (Wienert et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference from ChIP-Seq results with citation to Wienert et al., 2019

claim: FANCD2 has a conserved function as a histone chaperone.
source: The conserved function of FANCD2 as a histone chaperone (Sato et al., 2012; Higgs et al., 2018) may even be directly linked to displacement of nucleosomes as filamentous arrays extend into break-adjacent chromatin.
evidence: Supported by citations to Sato et al., 2012; Higgs et al., 2018

claim: BRCA1:BARD1 was initially thought to be the E3 for FANCD2 monoubiquitination because it co-immunoprecipitates FANCD2 and FANCD2 does not form nuclear foci after damage in BRCA1-deficient cells.
source: BRCA1:BARD1 was initially thought to be the E3 for FANCD2 monoubiquitination, because it co-immunoprecipitates FANCD2, and FANCD2 does not form nuclear foci after damage in BRCA1-deficient cells (Raghunandan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raghunandan et al., 2015

claim: FANCD2 monoubiquitination does occur in BRCA1-deficient cells, but it is uncoupled from FANCD2 foci formation.
source: However, in various assays it was later shown that FANCD2 monoubiquitination does occur in BRCA1-deficient cells, but it is uncoupled from FANCD2 foci formation (Jacquemont and Taniguchi, 2007; Moriel-Carretero et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jacquemont and Taniguchi, 2007; Moriel-Carretero et al., 2017

claim: DAN protein forms a rigid collaborative filament that reduces DNA accessibility during anoxia in prokaryotes.
source: Filamentous structures on DNA play a genome protective role in prokaryotes: eg DAN protein forms a rigid collaborative filament that reduces accessibility during anoxia (Lim et al., 2013), while the Vibrio cholera protein ParA2 forms protective filamentous structures on DNA during segregation (Hui et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lim et al., 2013

claim: Vibrio cholera protein ParA2 forms protective filamentous structures on DNA during segregation.
source: Filamentous structures on DNA play a genome protective role in prokaryotes: eg DAN protein forms a rigid collaborative filament that reduces accessibility during anoxia (Lim et al., 2013), while the Vibrio cholera protein ParA2 forms protective filamentous structures on DNA during segregation (Hui et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hui et al., 2010

claim: The coating of ssDNA by RPA in eukaryotes protects DNA from the activity of nucleases and directs the specific activity of others.
source: The coating of ssDNA by RPA in eukaryotes, also protect DNA from the activity of nucleases, and directs the specific activity of others (de Laat et al., 1998; Chen et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to de Laat et al., 1998; Chen et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2017

claim: FANCIub:D2ub arrays may have a stabilizing role on newly synthesized dsDNA at a stalled replication fork.
source: We propose that a FANCIub:D2ub arrays may have a similar stabilizing role on newly synthesized dsDNA at a stalled replication fork.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings and comparison to other systems

claim: Filamentous DNA-clamped Iub:D2ub could prevent access to DNA by MRE11 and DNA2 nucleases.
source: In particular, we hypothesize that filamentous DNA-clamped Iub:D2ub could prevent access to DNA by MRE11 and DNA2 nucleases and prevent aberrant ligation of broken DNA to other parts of the genome by non-homologous end-joining.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings

claim: The tight binding of FANCIub:D2ub to dsDNA at stalled replication forks may prevent the branch migration of replication forks and inhibit their spontaneous or helicase-mediated reversal.
source: Second, the tight binding of FANCIub:D2ub to dsDNA, when localized to stalled replication forks, may also prevent the branch migration of replication forks and inhibit their spontaneous or helicase-mediated reversal (Neelsen and Lopes, 2015).
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings with citation to Neelsen and Lopes, 2015

claim: Reversed forks are the substrate for degradation by DNA2 and WRN nuclease activities.
source: Reversed forks are the substrate for degradation by DNA2 and WRN nuclease activities, providing a hypothetical link between the activities of FANCD2-monoubiquitination and the nuclease activity of DNA2 and WRN (Thangavel et al., 2015; Sidorova et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Thangavel et al., 2015; Sidorova et al., 2013

claim: Iub:D2ub arrays may locally suppress non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) factors.

claim: FANCD2, FANCI, and components of the FA core complex were identified in a genome-wide screen for genes that promote templated repair over NHEJ.
source: FANCD2, FANCI, and components of the FA core complex were identified amongst relatively few other factors, in a genome-wide screen for genes that promote templated repair over NHEJ (Richardson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Richardson et al., 2017

claim: Stabilization of RAD51 filaments is an in vitro property of ID2.
source: Stabilization of RAD51 filaments, required for HR, is also an in vitro property of ID2 (Sato et al., 2016), suggesting Iub:D2ub filamentous arrays may exist adjacent to or coincident with RAD51 filaments in cells, in order to provide a polarity to the homologous recombination reaction without loss or gain of genomic sequences.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sato et al., 2016

claim: Fanci and Fancd2 have common and distinct functions in mouse models of Fanconi anemia.
source: Fanci and Fancd2 have common and distinct functions in mouse models of Fanconi anemia (Dubois et al., 2019), while the double knockout of FANCI and FANCD2 has an unexpectedly distinct phenotype compared to single knockouts in human cells (Thompson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dubois et al., 2019
